condition.question: Section 28 point 4: in scripts/stage1/representation_pass.py, does each row's features depend only on that row (one unbatched forward per row, no batch-dependent normalization or padding effect)?
finding: representation_pass.py:113-127 read_states: each call runs one forward of one row only. Line 118 builds ids = torch.tensor([list(input_ids)]), a batch of one with no padding. Line 119 calls model(input_ids=ids, output_hidden_states=True) with no attention mask and no other row. Lines 123-126 read only h[0] at that row's own positions (positions(), :103-110, from the row's length and n_prompt).

representation_pass.py:352-355: model.eval() (dropout off), torch.no_grad() and model.disable_adapter() (the untuned model) are set once for the whole pass. No state is carried from one row to the next. Each norm is per token (the summaries give layout.final_norm Olmo2RMSNorm), and no step uses statistics over the batch.

representation_pass.py:357-367: the anchor states, anchor_means (:130-142, a sum in the bank's file order then a division), the directions and CAS come only from the pinned anchor bank. They are computed before any scored row, so no scored row changes them.

representation_pass.py:371-378: each row's line uses its own read_states (:372). The cosines are against the anchor means (:373-374) and css uses the anchor directions (:375-376). The line holds only id, source, unit, n_prompt, n_tokens, cos_harmful, cos_safe and css (:377-378).

representation_pass.py:338-349: encode_train encodes each pool item alone (:344). A refused item is counted and skipped (:345-348). An item id that repeats a scored id refuses the whole pass (:341-342). D-3 refuses repeated ids across the union for the same reason.

representation_pass.py:388: the rows file is the join of json_line(line), one line per row, in the order the rows dict was filled: dev rows first (:333-336), then the pools in command-line order, each in item order. So one pools-only pass over s3_safe then s3_orig writes the s3_safe lines and then the s3_orig lines. These are the same bytes as the union, because each line depends only on its row and the anchor means.

W1 tests that already check this: scripts/stage1/tests/test_representation_pass.py test_v_every_forward_is_one_unpadded_row (every hidden-state forward has batch 1 and no mask, or an all-ones mask), test_fc_every_hidden_state_forward_runs_in_eval_mode, and test_deterministic_and_text_free.
condition.evidence_on_cpu: test_d3_s3_union.py test_each_pass_gives_a_row_the_same_bytes_whatever_else_it_scores and test_the_union_rows_are_one_pools_only_pass_over_both_pools_byte_for_byte: on the engine's fixture model, an s3_safe row has the same bytes whether it is scored beside the dev units and another pool or beside s3_orig. The union is the single pass's rows file byte for byte.
condition.evidence_on_the_real_passes: Read from the two summaries' text-free fields only. Every field D-3 compares is equal: kind, version, requirement, layout (olmo2, 16 layers, 2048, Olmo2RMSNorm), conventions, reads, untuned, transformers 4.56.2, anchors 64/64, pool_pins a33e9664..., the whole datashield block (CAS and direction norm at all 17 indices, bit-equal), provenance (script, script fb62bcaa, s1common 930c8ea5, settings a555fd89, engine 472fc7f6, Python 3.12.3, numpy 2.2.6), the inputs (anchor file, prepared manifest, recipe file 464708c9..., pool pins), Gate C's index, read and rule, and device cuda on both. The equal datashield block means both passes computed the same anchor-derived numbers.
condition.limit: 'Equals one pass' holds up to the run-to-run reproducibility of the pass itself. A single CUDA pass run twice could already differ in the last bits if its kernels are not deterministic. Each union row comes from exactly one real forward. The bit-equal datashield block is evidence, not proof, that the two passes' anchor means (reads a, b, c, d) are the same: CAS uses the read-b states and the direction norm uses the read-c means.

item_1_design.outputs: In --work (absent or empty): representation_rows.jsonl, the main pass's s3_safe lines then the pools-only pass's s3_orig lines, each line's bytes unchanged; and representation_pass.json, the main pass's summary with pools = [main's s3_safe entry, the pools-only pass's s3_orig entry], rows = the union's (file, SHA-256, lines, by_source), and a 'd3' block (both sources' summary and rows SHA-256s, pools, counts, both records' SHA-256s, the rule, the reference, the checked fields, and the D-3 script, settings, W1 manifest, scorer and engine hashes). Every other field is the main pass's, unchanged. Then score_s3_datarx.py runs as a private module (not in sys.modules; sys.path is restored after its load) through its own main() with --rows and --summary set to the union files (PATH:SHA), --s-pool-record and --answers-record as given, and --out. Its exit code is D-3's. If the scorer refuses, the two text-free union files stay in --work and --out stays empty (tested).
item_1_design.union_summary_choice: pools lists only s3_safe and s3_orig, not plant and decoy, because the union rows hold only those two pools. This is exactly the pools list that one pools-only pass over both pools writes (tested). The main pass's full pool list is kept in d3.sources.main.pools. gate_c, costs and provenance stay the main pass's, as section 28 point 2 says ('the main pass's summary with both pools listed'), and d3.from_the_main_pass states this.
alternatives_and_why: Re-serialising the union rows from parsed objects was rejected. Copying each line's bytes keeps section 28 point 2's 'each unchanged' and the byte-for-byte claim, and the json_line check proves the bytes are REQ-3's own form.

Calling the scorer's build() in memory was rejected in favour of its own main() with the union files written first. That is the scorer 'unchanged' on PATH:SHA inputs: it re-reads and re-hashes the files.

Not comparing the datashield block was rejected. The equal block is the only text-free cross-pass check that both passes computed the same anchor means, and it holds on the real passes (checked from their summaries). If it ever differs, D-3 refuses and section 28 point 5's fallback applies.

Patterned on D-1 and D-2: by-path load after the manifest check, a private module, settings pinned by literal, a fixture guard and its own mutation spec and runner. Small helpers (parse_hashed, read_hashed, manifest_entries) are copied, not imported from D-2, so the package does not depend on D-2.

item_2_design.rule: plan_tool.release_next: when the launch before has hosts that are neither done nor moved, release now calls rules.guard_off_record(HERE), the same re-hashed check launch.py and host.py use. If the result is None (no record, or a record whose file changed or is gone), the old refusal stays exactly as it was ('block X: launch k-1's hosts are not done (host)'). If a record holds, the hosts launch is released and {launch, open_hosts, guard_off_sha256, utc} is added to the block's released_early. release() returns it and writes it to operator-actions.jsonl. The order (one launch per release), check_planned_group_a (plan conformance) and every gate in release_hosts still run.
item_2_design.decision_for_the_lead: A judge launch still waits, with the guard off too, until every earlier launch's hosts are done or moved. Reason: block_a_done (plan_tool.py block_a_done) counts a released judge launch as the judge job's completion record. Released early, it would mark HarmBench and Granite as done before the units they judge exist. Section 28's text covers 'the next launch' in general; this keeps G5's completion accounting meaningful. A one-line change lifts it if the lead wants judges included.
item_2_design.need_note: rules.funding_need_usd still prices one launch at a time (running spend plus the next launch's caps). With launches in parallel, the balance held at one moment can exceed the recorded need. The total cap-based spend is unchanged. Section 28 leaves the balance to the user; the README now says this.
item_2_design.docs: The plan_tool.py docstring (the release command line and the release paragraph) and README section E now describe the rule.
